c.tagline: Faded grandeur, classic cars, and salsa on every corner.

taxi.color: yellow (state Cubataxi) or classic American cars
taxi.fareNote: Most tourist taxis negotiate a fixed fare upfront in USD/CUP cash before departure; official yellow Cubataxi cabs sometimes use meters but fixed pricing is far more common.

emergency.note: Tourist-specific assistance also available via Asistur at +53 7 866-4499; response times and resources are limited compared to North America/Europe.

avoid.reason: Low violent crime; petty theft/scams in Habana Vieja and Centro Habana — mind bags and touts (jineteros)

hood_desc: The historic UNESCO-listed core with cobblestone plazas, colonial architecture, and the highest concentration of restored hotels, restaurants, and museums; best for first-time visitors who want to walk everywhere.

A leafy, seafront district of 1950s mansions, university buildings, and the iconic Malecón and Hotel Nacional; suits travelers wanting a residential feel with easy access to nightlife and casas particulares.
A grittier, densely populated area right by Old Havana with cheap paladares and local life on display; good for budget travelers who don't mind a rougher edge and lots of street noise.

An upscale, leafy diplomatic and business district west of the Almendares River with modern hotels, embassies, and better infrastructure; suits business travelers and those wanting quiet and reliability.

A working port town across Havana Bay reached by ferry, home to Che Guevara's mausoleum-adjacent sites and a laid-back, less touristy vibe; suits day-trippers or those seeking a quieter, cheaper base.
lodging: Gran Hotel Manzana Kempinski La Habana
Casa particular near Regla ferry dock

water.note: Avoid tap water; drink only bottled or boiled water.

transit.pay: Fares on regular city buses are paid in cash CUP directly to the driver or a conductor (very low fixed fare); the harbor ferry to Regla/Casablanca is also a small cash CUP fare paid at the dock. Tourist hop-on-hop-off buses (Habana Bus Tour) are paid in USD/CUP cash or card at kiosks.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly 5:00-24:00 with reduced frequency at night; the ferry operates until around 22:00-23:00; taxis and classic-car cabs are the main night option.
transit.note: Public buses are often extremely crowded and unpredictable due to fuel shortages; most visitors rely on taxis, pre-arranged transfers, or walking within neighborhoods rather than city buses.

train: Ferrocarriles de Cuba national rail from Havana Central Station (limited, slow service to other provinces)
ferry: Havana Bay ferry to Regla and Casablanca

tip.r: Service staff earn very low state wages in CUP, so tips (ideally in cash USD or EUR) are a major part of income; 10% is typical at restaurants, and small tips for musicians, guides, and casa particular hosts are strongly expected.
